entities.name: Mont-Saint-Michel Abbey
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Mont Saint-Michel Abbey on its tidal island off the Normandy coast, founded in 966 CE by Richard I of Normandy as a Benedictine abbey, is one of France's most recognizable monuments and an extraordinary example of medieval military and religious architecture built on a granite island that becomes accessible only at low tide. The Abbey was a major pilgrimage destination throughout the Middle Ages, attracting hundreds of thousands of pilgrims who crossed the dangerous tidal sands — many drowned — to reach what was called 'Saint Michael in peril of the sea.'

The island had been associated with the Archangel Michael since Bishop Aubert's 708 CE vision; the Benedictine abbey was established in 966. Through the medieval period, the abbey was expanded and rebuilt in Romanesque and Gothic styles while maintaining its defensive function — the island withstood English siege during the Hundred Years' War despite Normandy falling to the English. The Merveille (Marvel), the three-story Gothic building constructed 1211-1228, is one of medieval architecture's greatest achievements, combining monks' hall, guests' hall, knights' hall, cellars, and cloister in a seamless structure on the rock face.

Mont Saint-Michel was used as a prison from the Revolution through 1863. Its restoration by Viollet-le-Duc's student Edouard Corroyer in the 19th century, and the addition of a neogothic spire with Michael the Archangel at its apex in 1897, created the silhouette that 3.5 million annual visitors come to see today.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Mont Saint-Michel's thousand-year history as pilgrimage destination, military fortress, and Gothic architectural wonder — on its dramatic tidal island — makes it France's most complete expression of medieval civilization's integration of faith, art, and power.
